title: Environmental Sensors, Placement, Calibration and Data Quality

content.overview: Environmental numbers are only useful when the measurement represents the crop. Sensor location, shielding, calibration, airflow exposure, and logging interval can all change what a temperature or humidity reading means.

vocabulary.definition: Comparison and adjustment of a measuring instrument against a known reference or standard.
A systematic measurement error that consistently shifts readings away from the true condition.
A measurement position chosen to reflect the environment actually experienced by the crop rather than an atypical hot, cold, wet, or dry zone.

sections.title: Placement determines relevance
sections.body: A sensor near a dehumidifier outlet, wall, lamp, intake, or wet surface may report a local microclimate rather than the average crop environment. Placement should be selected to answer a defined question about the canopy.

sections.title: Calibration protects trend quality
sections.body: Two sensors can drift apart over time. Periodic comparison with a reliable reference helps distinguish real environmental change from instrument error.

sections.title: Logging reveals dynamics
sections.body: Short-term peaks, nighttime transitions, irrigation events, and equipment cycling can disappear inside a daily average. Logged data should preserve enough time resolution to reveal biologically meaningful patterns.

workedExamples: If one humidity sensor reads much drier than the others, compare its location and calibration before changing the room set point.
A room average can look acceptable while a sensor inside a dense canopy shows prolonged high humidity; investigate the local microclimate rather than relying only on the wall controller.
commonMistakes: Placing sensors where equipment exhaust directly affects them.
Assuming a new sensor cannot be biased.
Using a single daily average to evaluate short-term environmental stress.
content.practicalApplication: Map sensor locations, compare readings under the same conditions, document calibration checks, and review logged temperature and humidity around important transitions such as lights-on, lights-off, irrigation, and equipment cycling.
content.summary: Good environmental control starts with trustworthy measurements. Sensor placement, calibration, and logging context determine whether temperature, humidity, and VPD data actually describe the crop.
